item.title: Should space data centers run on solar panels, nuclear reactors or both?
item.description: The last few days we've been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently—maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI simulates electron hops over far longer times than conventional quantum calculations
item.description: To predict how a material will behave, we need to know which atoms are located where. This allows us, for example, to explain whether a material is suitable as a catalyst for certain chemical reactions. But often, that is not enough: even if all the atoms stay exactly where they are, the distribution of electric charge within the material can change dramatically. Electrons can jump from one atom to another, changing the forces between atoms as well as the material's chemical reactivity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Targeted conversion of carbon dioxide into chemical feedstocks: CO₂ helps shape its own catalyst
item.description: Electrochemists at the University of Duisburg-Essen have discovered through computer simulations that carbon dioxide (CO₂) helps shape the surface of its own catalyst when the catalyst is restructured using voltage pulses. The calculations suggest that this allows CO₂ to be converted preferentially into formic acid. The findings have been published in Advanced Functional Materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

The size, shape and orientation of the mineral grains that make them up can reveal how rocks formed, deformed and changed deep beneath the surface. However, collecting this information has traditionally required specialized equipment and time-consuming analysis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lab experiments suggest bat RSV can enter human cells, but existing antibodies block it
item.description: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes severe respiratory disease and is responsible for numerous deaths each year. A research team led by DZIF scientist Dr. Wendy K. Jo and DZIF scientist Dr. Jan Felix Drexler at Charité—University Medicine Berlin, as well as DZIF board member Dr. Thomas Pietschmann and Dr. Sibylle Haid from TWINCORE in Hanover, has now characterized a virus in West African fruit bats that is genetically distinct from known RSV variants but belongs to the same viral family as RSV. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research establishes fundamental complexity limit for quantum circuit optimization
item.description: Quantum circuit optimization is an important research area, as the computational resources required to execute quantum algorithms remain a major challenge. In particular, two-qubit operations are generally associated with higher error rates than single-qubit gates on current quantum hardware, making reducing the number of two-qubit gates an important objective. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fiber-optic sensing unearths surprising complexity in small California earthquake
item.description: More than 20,000 earthquakes are located worldwide each year, but the vast majority of those are small—many too small to be felt by humans. Scientists have historically assumed most of these small earthquakes break as small, circular ruptures in which the rocks in a fault slip past each other in a single, smooth motion, and the crack spreads outward from one point like a ripple in a pond, unlike the behavior of most major earthquakes. Fuente: Phys.org.
